what: Requires property tax notices and school and city bond-election pamphlets to show the tax cost for a $300,000 home, in addition to the smaller home values used now. The House version also added a $2 million commercial property example for city bond elections.
who: School districts, community college districts, cities, counties and other taxing districts; property owners who read these notices.
why: Business owners who own property would see a more realistic example of what a proposed tax increase or bond would cost them.
outcome: Vetoed by the Governor.

what: Exempts income from renting required college textbooks at bookstores from the state sales tax on rentals (transaction privilege tax).
who: Bookstores that rent textbooks required by state universities and community colleges, and the students who rent them.
why: Removes a tax on one line of business for campus and independent bookstores.
outcome: Signed into law.

what: Changes how renewable energy and battery storage equipment is valued for property taxes. Equipment owned by or under contract to a utility keeps a lower valuation if construction starts before 2030; other equipment is taxed at its full depreciated cost.
who: Owners of solar, wind and storage equipment, utilities, and the counties and school districts that collect property tax on it.
why: Affects property tax bills for businesses that own their own solar or storage systems.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: The budget's tax bill for fiscal year 2027. Among other things, it extends through June 2030 the fees and fund transfers that pay for modernizing the Department of Revenue's tax computer system.
who: The Department of Revenue, cities, counties and regional transportation authorities that pay the modernization fees.
why: The tax system modernization affects how businesses file and pay state sales and income taxes.
outcome: Signed into law.

what: The budget's main tax bill for 2026-2027. It updates Arizona's tax code to match 2025 federal tax changes, adds state deductions for tips and overtime pay, changes several tax credits, pauses new tax breaks for data centers from July 2026 to June 2029, and makes other income, sales and property tax changes.
who: Individual and business taxpayers, employers whose workers earn tips or overtime, and data center developers.
why: Changes what many small businesses and their employees owe in state income tax, starting with 2025 returns.
outcome: Signed into law.

what: Would have updated Arizona's tax code to match 2025 federal tax changes, added state deductions for tips and overtime, increased the dependent tax credit, and opted Arizona into a new federal tax credit for donations to school scholarship organizations.
who: Individual taxpayers, employers whose workers earn tips or overtime, and school scholarship organizations.
why: Most of the federal conformity changes were enacted instead through the budget tax bill, HB 4168.
outcome: Vetoed by the Governor.

what: A yearly clean-up of tax laws: fixes errors and outdated wording. Its one policy change removes the rule that cash equivalents and precious-metal bullion are sales-tax exempt only when sold to the final consumer.
who: The Department of Revenue and businesses that sell bullion, coins or cash equivalents.
why: Simplifies sales tax rules for dealers who sell bullion to other businesses.
outcome: Signed into law.

what: Clarifies that the location of the computer servers used to take an order does not decide where a sale happened for state sales tax, and defines "business location".
who: Retailers and other sellers that take orders online or remotely.
why: Affects which city's tax rate applies to a sale, which matters for small sellers filing in several cities.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: Would have given the Arizona Commerce Authority $100,000 to study the economic benefits of small modular nuclear reactors and data centers, including jobs, tax revenue and spin-off businesses.
who: The Arizona Commerce Authority and communities considering reactors or data centers.
why: The study would have estimated how many supplier and service businesses could grow up around these projects.
outcome: Did not get out of committee.

what: Changes how government agencies hire firms for construction and design work: lets them use cooperative purchasing agreements for job-order contracts, adjusts the construction-manager-at-risk process, adds "progressive design-build" as a method, and counts pipelines as horizontal construction.
who: State and local agencies that buy construction services, and contractors and design firms that bid on public work.
why: Changes the rules that small contractors and design firms follow to win public construction contracts.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: Directs the Arizona Commerce Authority to work on fuel supply and gas prices. The House version made lowering fuel prices the Authority's primary goal and ordered a study of cheaper fuel blends, new pipelines and refineries; the Senate version made fuel supply resilience one of its goals and created a Fuel Resiliency Task Force.
who: The Arizona Commerce Authority, the oil and gas industry, and drivers and businesses that buy fuel.
why: Fuel costs affect delivery, trucking, farming and service businesses.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: Would have created a House study committee to review the Arizona Commerce Authority's overseas trade offices. The committee would have ended in 2029.
who: The Arizona Commerce Authority and members of the House.
why: Trade offices help Arizona businesses find export customers.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: Makes the Arizona Commerce Authority's overseas trade offices depend on legislative funding instead of its board's decision. Funding must be based on research by the Authority, which must report each December on every office's activities.
who: The Arizona Commerce Authority and its trade offices.
why: Trade offices help small exporters; this changes who decides where they open and how they're reviewed.
outcome: Signed into law.

what: Would have added four legislators (the chairs and top minority members of the Senate Finance and House International Trade committees) to the Arizona Commerce Authority's board, as non-voting members.
who: The Arizona Commerce Authority's board.
why: Gives legislators a closer look at the state's main business development agency.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: Would have added four non-voting legislators to the Arizona Commerce Authority's board, required legislative funding and yearly reports for its trade offices, and continued the Arizona Competes program until July 2030.
who: The Arizona Commerce Authority and businesses that receive Arizona Competes grants.
why: Arizona Competes funds grants used to attract and grow businesses.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: Would have let cities, towns and counties set up a C-PACE program, which lets owners of commercial property finance building improvements (such as energy or water upgrades) through an assessment repaid with property taxes.
who: Local governments, commercial property owners and private lenders.
why: C-PACE gives business property owners another way to pay for upgrades without a traditional loan.
outcome: Did not get out of committee.

what: Would have given Arizona bidders a 1% edge over out-of-state bidders when state bids are tied, and matched any preference that another state gives its own bidders.
who: State purchasing agencies and businesses bidding on state contracts.
why: Would have helped Arizona businesses win tie-breaks for state contracts.
outcome: Did not get out of committee.

what: Would have added a new option for the Qualified Facilities tax credit, starting in 2027: $25,000 per qualified job created at a rural facility, for projects investing less than $2 billion.
who: Manufacturers and other employers building facilities in rural Arizona.
why: Would have made the credit easier to use for smaller rural projects.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: Lets a city, town or county create a tourism improvement area when lodging businesses petition for one. Lodging businesses in the area pay an assessment that a destination marketing organization uses to promote the area.
who: Hotels and other lodging businesses, local governments and tourism marketing groups.
why: Gives local lodging businesses a way to pool money for tourism marketing.
outcome: Signed into law.

what: Despite its title ("growth zones; housing and economic"), the House summary describes a bill letting cities and towns amend their adopted budget during the year to spend unexpected revenue, without raising taxes or fees.
who: Cities and towns.
why: Indirect: affects how local governments can spend new revenue during the year.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: The budget's commerce bill for 2026-2027. It continues the Arizona Competes Fund until July 2028 with $1.75 million a year from the lottery, and makes other commerce-related budget changes.
who: The Arizona Commerce Authority and businesses that receive Arizona Competes grants.
why: Keeps the state's main business attraction and expansion grant fund running.
outcome: Signed into law.

what: Rewritten during the session: despite its title about the Arizona Commerce Authority's board, the final version dealt with local ballot measures. It would have applied strict review to city, town and county initiatives and referendums and added rules for petition circulators, including registering paid and out-of-state circulators.
who: Cities, towns, counties and groups that gather signatures for local ballot measures.
why: Not a business bill in its final form; listed because of its original title.
outcome: Vetoed by the Governor.

what: Exempts dental schools, dental therapy schools and dental hygiene schools from registering as business entities with the State Board of Dental Examiners, and lets their students and faculty practice in school clinics.
who: Dental and dental hygiene schools and their students and faculty.
why: Narrow: affects dental training programs, not dental practices in general.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: The Senate's version of the budget commerce bill. It contained the same Arizona Competes Fund continuation as HB 4157, which became law instead.
who: The Arizona Commerce Authority.
why: See HB 4157.
outcome: Did not get out of committee.

what: Would have barred cities and towns from requiring mobile food vendors to get a local permit or license. Counties could still require one.
who: Food trucks and other mobile food vendors, and cities and towns.
why: Would have removed a layer of local licensing for food truck owners who work in several cities.
outcome: Vetoed by the Governor.

what: Would have required cities, towns and counties to set standard fees for towing cars from private property, added rules for those tows and for releasing towed vehicles, and created a heavy-duty truck towing study committee.
who: Towing companies, property owners, drivers and local governments.
why: Would have changed how towing businesses set prices and operate.
outcome: Vetoed by the Governor.

what: Would have let cities, towns and counties cap overnight occupancy in short-term rentals and suspend a rental's permit more easily after violations.
who: Short-term and vacation rental owners, guests and local governments.
why: Many short-term rental hosts run small businesses; this would have tightened local rules on them.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: Would have revised the rules for becoming a certified public accountant, including changes to the education and experience requirements for first-time applicants, and changed the Board of Accountancy's duties.
who: CPA applicants, accounting firms and the Board of Accountancy.
why: See SB 1181, which became law with similar changes.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: Would have added a definition of "apprenticeship" to state workforce law: paid, supervised on-the-job training combined with classroom instruction, following U.S. Department of Labor standards.
who: The Department of Economic Security, employers and apprenticeship programs.
why: A clear definition can make it easier for employers to set up recognized apprenticeships.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: Would have let cities offer a faster plan-review and permitting process for workforce housing projects and exempted those projects from the state's share of the sales tax on construction contracting. It also changed rules for industrial development authority bonds.
who: Housing developers, contractors and cities.
why: Faster permits and lower taxes for builders and contractors on workforce housing.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: Limits how cities and towns charge development fees: they can't base fees for single-family homes on size or number of bedrooms unless they already did, and a new or higher fee can't be charged for 24 months on projects whose plans are already approved.
who: Home builders, commercial and industrial developers, and cities and towns.
why: Gives builders more predictable costs once their plans are approved.
outcome: Signed into law.

what: Starting in 2028, requires a state license from the Department of Liquor Licenses and Control to make or distribute alternative nicotine products (such as nicotine pouches) in Arizona, and sets sales, marketing and enforcement rules, including for sales to people under 21.
who: Manufacturers, distributors and retailers of alternative nicotine products.
why: New licensing and compliance rules for convenience stores, smoke shops and distributors.
outcome: Signed into law.

what: Starting in 2027, creates alternative ways to qualify as a certified public accountant and updates the Board of Accountancy's powers, including oversight of CPA firms.
who: CPA applicants, accounting firms and the Board of Accountancy.
why: Could widen the pool of CPAs that small businesses rely on.
outcome: Signed into law.

what: Adopts the Uniform Assignment for Benefit of Creditors Act. It sets rules for a business or person to hand its assets to a trustee (an "assignee"), who sells them and pays creditors in a set order, as an alternative to bankruptcy.
who: Struggling businesses, their creditors and the professionals who handle these assignments.
why: Gives failing small businesses a clearer, often cheaper way to wind down than bankruptcy.
outcome: Signed into law.

what: Sets rules for solar installations: contractors must check that a roof can support the panels and recommend a roofing inspection. It also adds requirements for solar sales and lease agreements and what sales pitches must disclose.
who: Solar contractors, solar sales companies and homeowners.
why: New steps and paperwork for solar installers, many of which are small businesses.
outcome: Signed into law.

what: Updates many liquor laws, mostly starting in 2027: changes wording from "manufacture" to "produce", lets cities choose whether to tax liquor sales, drops federal food-safety rule requirements for licensed producers, and other changes.
who: Breweries, distilleries, wineries, bars, restaurants and cities.
why: Affects the rules for craft producers and other liquor licensees.
outcome: Signed into law.

what: Would have let the Administrative Rules Oversight Committee review whether a state agency's rule, practice or policy goes beyond what the law allows it to do.
who: State agencies and the businesses they regulate.
why: A route for challenging agency rules that small businesses see as overreach.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: Would have reorganized parts of the Industrial Commission of Arizona: ended its licensing of private employment offices, renamed its ombudsman a Resource Officer, and moved boiler safety into its own division.
who: The Industrial Commission, employers and staffing agencies.
why: Changes how employers deal with the agency that handles workplace safety and workers' compensation.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: Continues the Barbering and Cosmetology Board until 2034 and lowers the maximum fees it can charge for licenses, such as $100 to $80 for a personal license and $250 to $200 for a salon license application.
who: Barbers, cosmetologists, salons and barbershops.
why: Lowers licensing costs for salon and barbershop owners and their staff.
outcome: Signed into law.

what: Bars cities and counties from deliberately delaying permits for single-family home construction. The Attorney General can enforce it, with a $5,000 penalty per violation, and builders can get a fast court review.
who: Home builders, property owners, cities and counties.
why: Protects small builders from costly permit delays.
outcome: Signed into law.

what: Would have created a marijuana producer license starting in 2029, with early applications limited to businesses already growing under contract with a dispensary. It needed a three-fourths vote because it amends a voter-approved law.
who: Marijuana growers, dispensaries and the Department of Health Services.
why: Would have let contract growers hold their own license.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: Would have required cities and counties to give written notice before imposing an exaction (a required fee, land dedication or improvement) on a development, and let the applicant ask for an individualized explanation of it before appealing.
who: Developers, property owners, cities and counties.
why: Would have given property owners a clearer basis to question development requirements.
outcome: Vetoed by the Governor.

what: Rewritten during the session: despite its title about sick leave, the final version would have given the Department of Public Safety $4.75 million for operating costs and let it hire its own lawyers through 2026.
who: The Department of Public Safety.
why: Not a business bill in its final form; listed because of its original title.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: Would have given AHCCCS (Arizona's Medicaid agency) $5 million to fund a nonprofit that trains allied health care workers, such as medical assistants and technicians.
who: AHCCCS, health care training nonprofits and health care employers.
why: Would have grown the pool of trained workers for clinics and other health care employers.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.

what: Would have funded a $300,000 workforce study for Coconino County communities affected by the Navajo Generating Station closure and created a study committee on coal-impacted communities.
who: Communities near the closed coal plant, workers and local businesses.
why: Aimed at rebuilding jobs and businesses in communities that lost the plant.
outcome: Passed at least one chamber but did not become law.
